common_name: Wild Betel Leaf (La Lot, Cha Plu)

planting.note: Root 4–6 inch stem cuttings in moist potting mix or set divisions out after all danger of frost, into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in shade to deep partial shade; this low, spreading Southeast Asian groundcover scorches and stalls in direct sun or dry soil.

directions: Set rooted cuttings or rhizome divisions in humus-rich, constantly moist soil in full to partial shade; a thin bark or leaf mulch keeps the shallow, creeping stems from drying out between waterings. Piper sarmentosum spreads as a low groundcover of heart-shaped, glossy, peppery-aromatic leaves used fresh as a wrap for Thai miang kham and grilled in Vietnamese cha la lot, so keep harvesting young leaves to encourage bushy new growth rather than flowering spikes. It dies back hard below about 40°F, so gardeners outside zone 9–11 grow it in containers that overwinter indoors near a bright, humid window. Divide congested clumps every year or two in spring to renew vigor and generate new plants for sharing.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN-Global)

planting.note: Press broken stem fragments or rooted divisions into very well-drained, lean, dry to average, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to light shade at any point in the growing season; white stonecrop roots from the smallest piece wherever it touches soil.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining, lean soil in full sun to light shade; white stonecrop resents wet feet and heavy clay far more than it minds neglect or poor fertility. Tiny, tightly packed, bead-like blue-green leaves flush deep red-bronze under summer heat and drought stress, then carry flat clusters of small starry white flowers over the mat in early summer that draw bees and small butterflies. It roots and spreads readily from broken stem pieces, making it an easy, tough choice for green roofs, gravel gardens, wall crevices, and dry slopes where turf and border perennials fail. Shear back hard after bloom if the mat becomes leggy or thin in the center, and divide congested patches in spring to keep it dense.

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of warm, fertile, well-drained soil once soil has warmed past 70°F and frost danger has passed; egusi is grown for its oil- and protein-rich seed rather than sweet flesh, so let fruit fully mature and dry on the vine before harvest.

directions: Sow in hills of warm, well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing vines to sprawl across at least 6 feet of row; egusi is a distinct culinary melon from dessert watermelon, grown throughout West Africa for its flat, oil-rich seeds that are dried, ground, and used to thicken egusi soup and stews. The round, pale green fruit has bland, unpalatably bitter to fibrous flesh that is discarded — do not harvest young for eating like watermelon. Leave fruit on the vine well past the point a watermelon would be picked, until the rind dulls and the vine begins to dry back, then split fruits open and ferment or wash the pulp away to recover the flat white seeds for drying. Rotate away from other cucurbits each year to limit vine borer and powdery mildew buildup.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN-Global)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed thickly 1/4 inch deep into warm, moisture-retentive soil after last frost; white jute is a close relative of molokhia (Corchorus olitorius) grown both as a fiber crop and, when picked young, as a mild potherb in Bangladeshi and West African kitchens.

directions: Broadcast seed thickly into warm, fertile, consistently moist soil, since dense stands both suppress weeds and are the standard method for fiber production; thin or transplant survivors to a few inches apart for leaf harvest instead. Pinch or cut young shoots and the topmost tender leaves regularly starting around 5–6 weeks to keep plants leafy and to delay the tough, fibrous stem growth that signals the shift toward fiber-stage maturity; cooked leaves have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture similar to okra. If left unharvested for fiber, stalks are cut at the base once the lower leaves yellow, then retted in water to separate the bast fiber. White jute tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic flooding far better than most leaf greens, making it a reliable warm-season crop through the Gulf Coast summer.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN-Global)

planting.note: Broadcast fine seed on a firm, weed-free seedbed after last frost and rake in lightly, no more than 1/4 inch deep; niger's small, oil-rich achenes are the main ingredient of commercial 'nyjer' finch seed and the plant also serves as a quick-establishing pollinator and wildlife food plot cover.

directions: Broadcast fine seed onto a firm, weed-suppressed seedbed and rake in shallowly, since niger germinates and establishes fast enough on its own to out-compete most warm-season weeds. Plants form a branching, sunflower-family stalk topped with small yellow composite flowers that are heavily worked by bees and other pollinators through late summer, followed by tiny black seeds prized by finches and other seed-eating birds. Mow or roll at flowering to terminate as a soil-building green manure, or let seed heads dry fully on the stalk before combining or hand-stripping if growing for birdseed. Because it is frost-tender and shallow-rooted, niger is best used as a fast summer-only cover between spring and fall cash crops rather than for winter soil protection.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN-Global)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed directly in fall so winter cold and moisture break dormancy naturally, into very well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly, poor to average soil in full sun; sea holly forms a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established, so pot-grown starts should be set out young.

directions: Sow in fall in loose, sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun so seed overwinters and germinates with spring warmth, or set out young pot-grown plants while still small, since the long taproot makes older sea holly nearly impossible to move successfully. Thistle-like, powder-blue to silvery leaves edged with spines surround dense, steel-blue, cone-shaped flower heads on branching stems from midsummer into fall, drawing bees and other pollinators and holding color well when cut and dried. Native to Atlantic and Mediterranean coastal dunes, it is exceptionally salt- and wind-tolerant and thrives in the same lean, gritty, dry conditions that ruin most border perennials, making it well suited to beach and xeriscape plantings. Avoid rich soil, extra watering, or winter wet, all of which shorten its life and weaken the naturally compact, silvery habit.

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; poet's laurel is exceptionally slow to establish and is almost always propagated by division of mature clumps rather than seed.

directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, mulching well since roots resent drying out; poet's laurel is an Asparagaceae relative of butcher's broom grown not for flowers but for its arching stems of glossy, dark green, leaf-like cladodes that are a mainstay of the florist trade for their remarkable vase life. Tiny greenish flowers in spring are followed, on pollinated plants, by orange-red berries that persist through winter and add interest to the deep-shade planting. Growth is very slow, with clumps taking several years to reach mature size, so treat new plantings as a long-term investment and avoid disturbing established clumps once they are settled in. It tolerates dry shade and heavy shade better than nearly any other broadleaf evergreen, making it valuable under mature trees where little else will grow.
